title: Cohorted Headroom Orchestrator and Degradation Ops PRD (WIP)
content:
Summary:

This PRD proposes the Cohorted Headroom Orchestrator (CHO) — an autoscaling and graceful-degradation subsystem for Dedicated pools that groups tenants into operational cohorts and manages headroom, ephemeral-burst credits, and staged degradation lanes. The goal is to improve predictable throughput and fairness under transient demand spikes while preserving per-tenant SLOs where possible.

Why we need CHO (problem statement):
- Customers buy Dedicated capacity for predictable throughput, but short spikes and noisy tenants still cause tail latency and noisy-neighbor behavior.
- Existing per-tenant reservations are inflexible and either over-provision (waste) or lead to hard preemption during spikes.
- We lack a unified operator-friendly pattern for: 1) borrowing spare capacity across low-risk tenants, 2) gracefully degrading lower-fidelity lanes, and 3) isolating noisy tenants while minimizing customer-visible failures.

Goals (measurable):
- Reduce 95th-percentile token latency degradation during global 20%+ traffic spikes by 30% for reserved-capacity customers on average (simulated workloads).
- Decrease emergency preemptions (hard evictions) by 40% year-over-year for Dedicated pools participating in CHO.
- Provide operators and tenants with clear observability: cohort-level headroom, credit balance, degradation status.

Non-goals:
- Not intended to replace long-term reservation contracts or billing models.
- Not a general-purpose multi-tenant scheduler — focused on Dedicated pool-level headroom management and tenant-facing controls.

Key concepts and vocabulary:
- Cohort: a small group of tenants that share a headroom budget and have similar risk characteristics (e.g., internal alpha customers, low-latency enterprise, batch-heavy startups). Cohorts are configurable by the account owner and by ops onboarding rules.
- Headroom: pooled spare compute capacity within a pool/cohort that can be allocated temporarily to tenants during bursts. Measured in GPU-concurrency-equivalent units.
- Burst Credit (ephemeral): per-tenant short-lived credits that allow consumption above reservation; drawn from cohort headroom and subject to rate/volume limits and decay.
- Degradation Lane: a predefined fallback path that reduces compute/cost/perf fidelity under pressure (e.g., switch to smaller model variant, quantized replica, lower context length).
- Isolation Fence: a rapid containment action that moves a tenant to a constrained lane or sandbox to prevent cross-tenant impact.

High-level proposal:
1) Cohorting & Policy: Tenants on a Dedicated pool are grouped into cohorts. Admin-visible cohort policies include headroom allocation, max burst-per-minute, per-tenant weight, and degradation hierarchy.
2) Headroom Orchestration: The CHO runs an autoscaler-like controller that maintains a running estimate of available headroom, predicted short-term demand, and safe borrow limits per cohort. Headroom is replenished by normal scale-up and decays over time as credits are used.
3) Burst Credit Issuance: Tenants can consume ephemeral burst credits when they exceed reservation. Credits draw from cohort headroom and are metered for billing and throttling.
4) Graceful Degradation: When cohort headroom is low and predicted pressures persist, CHO triggers degradation lanes by priority: 1) reduce concurrency for opportunistic tenants, 2) route to a quantized/fast model variant, 3) apply context-length caps, 4) if needed, isolate noisy tenant in a sandboxed lane.
5) Operator Controls & Rollback: Operators can set cohort-level SLAs, enable emergency evacuation, or perform targeted fence actions. All actions produce audit logs and annotated traces.

Autoscaling and prediction model (overview):
- Running estimator uses exponential smoothing over recent CPU/GPU utilization, request arrival rate, and median sequence length to predict next-minute demand distribution per cohort.
- Controller computes a safety budget: safety_budget = max(reserved_headroom * alpha, predicted_peak * beta) where alpha/beta tuned per pool class.
- Decision rules: issue burst credits if (predicted_headroom >= credit_request) AND (cohort_credit_balance >= min_balance). Evict/penalize if sustained > threshold for N minutes.

Burst options (designs considered):
- Soft-credit model (CHO default): ephemeral credits tracked per tenant, soft throttles (queue) when exhausted. Credits decay slowly (e.g., 10%/hour).
- Escrowed pre-warm slots: temporarily spin up small pre-warmers paid from headroom to reduce cold-starts; limited in burstable pools.
- Opportunistic borrowing: lower-priority tenants allowed to borrow beyond credit at heavily discounted performance (background lane) until eviction.

Isolation controls and safety fences:
- Fast containment API: /v1/pools/{p}/tenants/{t}/fence with actions: throttle | quarantine | degrade-to-variant | route-off.
- Fence triggers: anomalous token/sec, degraded tail latency, or external alert.
- Soft-fence mode: apply rate-limits and lower concurrency but keep routes active; hard-fence moves traffic to sandboxed executors.

Tenant experience and API changes (surface):
- New fields in Dedicated pool config: cohort_name, burst_credit_limit, degradation_profile, isolation_policy.
- SDK: fetch cohort_status with headroom_balance, credit_balance, degradation_state.
- Billing: ephemeral credits billed at burst rate; optional invoice summaries grouped by cohort.

Operator UX and console changes:
- Cohort dashboard: headroom heatmap, credit burn rate, active degradation lanes, per-tenant risk scores, recent fence actions.
- Runbook button: trigger emergency slow-down or cohort-wide prewarm.

Telemetry and SLOs to capture:
- cohort_headroom_bytes/time-series, cohort_credit_balance, credit_issuance_events, degradation_events, fence_actions, preemption_count, 95/99 token latency per tenant and cohort.
- Alerting: cohort_headroom < 10% for > 2 minutes, sustained credit burn > X tokens/minute triggers inspection.

Simulation & validation plan:
- Build a synthetic cohort simulator (prototype exists in linked repo) to test fairness across patterns: sawtooth spikes, correlated surges, single noisy tenant blasts.
- Define acceptance criteria: fewer than 2 hard evictions per thousand tenant-hours in simulated 30-day traces, and 95th latency target improvement compared to baseline autoscaler.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (internal): run CHO in simulation and shadow mode on small dedicated pools (QA clusters).
- Phase 1 (early access): opt-in for selected customers with low production risk (beta tenants), manual operator oversight, 2-week cadence.
- Phase 2 (graduated): enable automated cohort policies and billing; expand to more pools.

Operational concerns and edge cases:
- Billing disputes for billing spikes due to ephemeral credits — need clear UI/alerts and credit thresholds.
- Malicious tenants intentionally generating microbursts — require rapid automated fencing and penalties.
- Cross-region pools: headroom cannot migrate across regions; CHO must respect region boundaries.

Security & compliance notes:
- Audit trails for all fence and degradation actions stored for 90 days.
- Private deployments: CHO controller will run in customer control plane for Private mode; product will provide policy templates but not enforce data egress.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- Cohort sizing heuristics: static vs dynamic cohort rebalancing — dynamic rebalance reduces waste but increases churn and complexity.
- Billing model: should ephemeral credits be pre-purchased or pay-as-you-go? Pricing affects adoption.
- Degradation fidelity: how to choose default degradation sequence that balances quality vs latency across models?

Next steps / immediate work items:
- Priya: complete cohort simulator scenarios (due 2026-01-10).
- Diego: prototype headroom estimator and safety_budget heuristics (due 2025-12-20).
- Samir: console wireframes for cohort dashboard and fence actions (due 2026-01-05).
- Ops: identify 3 candidate early-access customers and collect traffic traces for simulation (due 2025-12-31).

Appendix — short example flows:
1) Single-tenant spike (tenanta): tenanta exceeds reservation by 3x for 90s; CHO issues ephemeral credits from cohort headroom, customer latency preserved, credits logged. If spike persists > 5 minutes, downgrade to quantized variant then fence if continues.
2) Correlated surge across cohort: CHO prioritizes tenants by weight, enforces per-tenant caps, invokes degradation lanes for opportunistic tenants, notifies ops.

Notes (informal / to-be-discussed):
- This feels like a hybrid between a financial credit model and SLO-aware autoscaler. Need input from pricing on acceptable discounting and from research on quantized variant quality regressions.
- Naming: cohort vs shard vs lane — I prefer cohort for operator mental model, but open to changes.
